content: The pleura is the thin membrane that lines the lungs and the chest cavity. Pleuritic pain, or pleurodynia, refers to discomfort originating from this lining, often experienced as chest or upper abdominal pain that worsens with breathing. Epidemic pleurodynia, however, is caused by a viral infection and produces pain similar to pleuritic pain, but the source of the discomfort is the chest muscles connecting the ribs. Until 1949, the cause of this condition was unknown. In 1872, Daae-Finsen described an outbreak of acute muscular rheumatism in a Norwegian community called Bamble, leading to the term Bamble disease. Later reports, published in Norwegian, continued to use this name. In 1933, Ejnar Sylvest presented a doctoral thesis on a Danish outbreak on Bornholm Island, naming it Bornholm disease myalgia epidemica, a term that has persisted. The disease is named after Bornholm Island, where early cases were documented. Notable outbreaks have occurred in Ohio (1936), Oxford (1951), Toronto (1958), and Singapore (1974). Despite the geographic and temporal separation of these epidemics, the disease's pattern and seasonal factors were often similar. Bornholm disease is caused primarily by group B coxsackieviruses, less commonly by group A coxsackieviruses or echoviruses. The infection leads to pain in the chest muscles that connect the ribs. The virus spreads through contact, particularly via saliva and feces, and outbreaks are more common in warm weather in temperate regions or year-round in tropical areas. After entering the body, the virus multiplies in the throat and intestines, then spreads to the chest wall muscles, abdominal muscles, and diaphragm, eventually reaching lymphatic tissues. The virus exploits autophagy to enhance its replication. The most common causative strains include Coxsackievirus B (especially B3 and B4) and Coxsackievirus A (types 4, 6, 9, and 10). Echovirus types 1, 6, 8, 9, and 19 have also been implicated. Coxsackievirus B is more frequently associated with respiratory complaints than Coxsackievirus A. The clinical presentation varies by age group and viral strain. Severe disease progression is rare but has been linked to Coxsackievirus B3. Bornholm disease is also known by other names, such as Devil's Grip, epidemic pleurodynia, and epidemic myalgia. Its diagnosis can be challenging due to the variety of names and its exclusion from initial differential diagnoses for chest pain. Extensive diagnostic workup is often required to rule out life-threatening conditions like acute coronary syndromes, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleurisy, appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, costochondritis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Epidemiologically, up to 90% of outbreaks occur in summer and early fall, with the disease primarily affecting individuals under 30 years old, though older adults can also be affected. Bornholm disease accounts for 20-40% of all non-cardiac chest pain cases. Pediatric studies have shown that Coxsackievirus A4, B3, and B4 are the most common causative agents. There is currently insufficient evidence to screen for Bornholm disease, but physical examinations and laboratory findings can support a viral diagnosis. Patients with Bornholm disease typically experience sudden, sharp, knife-like chest pain and fever lasting 4-7 days. Recovery is gradual, taking up to 10 days, with relapses being common. The disease is rarely fatal, and complications are uncommon but more likely in children. Potential complications include acute viral meningitis, orchitis, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy, pericarditis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Prognosis is generally excellent, with symptomatic treatment and bed rest being sufficient. In cases of orchitis, supportive measures like suspensory bandages may be helpful. Fever may be accompanied by headaches, and approximately 40% of patients report severe chest pain described as an iron grip around the rib cage, giving rise to the term Devil's Grip. Poor oral intake, weakness, and muscle fatigue are also common, and relapses are frequent despite quick recovery. Physical examination findings vary depending on the underlying cause. In cases caused by Coxsackievirus, symptoms may include oral ulcers, throat pain, diarrhea, and vomiting. Localized chest tenderness, abdominal rigidity, and guarding may complicate the examination. Pain can lead to tachycardia. Pulmonary symptoms may include pleural effusion, cough, rhinorrhea, and difficulty breathing. Fever may be associated with headaches and, in some cases, febrile seizures. Laboratory tests often reveal elevated inflammatory markers such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Changes in complete blood count (CBC) vary by viral strain. Leukocytosis is common, but Coxsackievirus A4 infections can result in white blood cell counts exceeding 15,000/µL. Coxsackievirus B3 has been associated with anemia and thrombocytopenia. Liver function tests (AST and ALT) may be elevated, but electrolyte changes are not typically observed. In cases of respiratory or cardiac complications, arterial blood gas and pulse oximetry may show abnormalities. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are often performed to rule out life-threatening conditions like myocardial infarction. Findings may include non-specific changes, such as T wave inversions, which resolve as the disease subsides. Myocardial infarction can be excluded due to the absence of ST changes. Chest X-rays may show pulmonary infiltrates in nearly half of all cases. Less common findings include patchy consolidation and pleural effusions. MRI can reveal muscle involvement, often as patchy thickened fascia and hyperintense muscles. Diagnostic studies for Bornholm disease are limited, and extensive testing is often performed to rule out cardiac conditions. Stool, blood, and throat samples may contain traces of the causative virus, which has also been detected in sewage and flies. MRI can show changes in muscle and fascia, and normal nerve conduction studies can help differentiate the disease from Guillain-Barré syndrome. Treatment primarily involves symptomatic management with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or heat application to affected muscles. In healthy individuals, pleurodynia is a self-limiting infection that resolves within a few days. Over-the-counter pain relievers are typically recommended, but narcotic pain medications may be used if necessary. Aspirin should not be given to children due to the risk of Reye's syndrome, a serious condition causing brain and liver injury during certain viral illnesses. Surgical intervention is rarely required, as the disease is usually self-limiting and responds to medical treatment. Surgery may be considered in cases of myocarditis unresponsive to other treatments. Primary prevention focuses on preventing the spread of the viruses that cause epidemic pleurodynia. Handwashing, especially before meals and after using the bathroom or changing diapers, is the most effective preventive measure. There is no vaccine for pleurodynia. Secondary prevention aims to prevent complications once the disease has developed. Measures include strict isolation, frequent handwashing, and good hygiene to prevent viral meningitis. Orchitis may be prevented by addressing underlying urinary tract infections, and hepatitis can be avoided through vaccination and safe eating habits. Pericarditis prevention may involve the use of aspirin and colchicine. Respiratory distress can be minimized by managing tidal volume, PEEP, FiO2, and reducing aspiration risk through proper positioning and oral hygiene. The treatment of Bornholm disease is cost-effective, as it primarily involves the use of NSAIDs, which are affordable and effective in managing inflammatory pain. For example, a bottle of ibuprofen containing 30 tablets costs less than $14 in the United States. Future research focuses on preventing Coxsackievirus infections, the most common cause of Bornholm disease. The virus is a non-enveloped, positive single-stranded RNA virus capable of forming an envelope by utilizing host membranes, which enhances its resistance. The relationship between Coxsackievirus infections and chronic diseases, such as autoimmune conditions, chronic myocarditis, diabetes, and chronic inflammatory myopathy, is of particular interest. Research is also exploring the effects of the virus in utero, as neonates may present with fetal myocarditis and neurodevelopmental delays, potentially due to meningitis and encephalitis.
